# How to Redesign Your Tasks to Work With AI (Instead of Fighting It)

We've all been there — staring at a blank document, wondering where to start. Whether it's an essay for a course, a report for work, or a project plan, the struggle is real. AI tools can now knock out a passable draft in seconds. So what's the point of doing the work yourself? Here's a smarter idea: instead of banning AI or pretending it doesn't exist, redesign the task so AI becomes part of the process — not the whole process.

## The old approach isn't really working

For a while, the default response to AI was simple: ban it. Schools blocked ChatGPT. Managers told staff not to use it. The thinking was that AI-generated work wasn't "real" work. But here's the catch — once a tool exists, people use it. Trying to pretend AI isn't there doesn't prepare anyone for the workplaces and lives they're heading into.

A more useful approach? Treat AI like a calculator (the tool that does the maths for you). Nobody says using a calculator means you can't do maths. The real skill is knowing which problem to solve, and what to do with the answer.

## How to redesign a task to use AI well

Here are three practical moves you can try today.

**1. Add a "thinking layer" before the writing.** Instead of asking AI to write the whole essay, ask it to argue against your draft. Try this prompt (the instruction you type to the AI): *"Here is my draft. What would a critical reader ask about it? Push back on my weakest points."* You do the thinking. AI stress-tests it.

**2. Make the process visible.** Ask AI to show its working. A better prompt is: *"Explain your reasoning step by step, then give me the final version."* This turns AI from a black box into a teaching tool. You can spot where its logic is shaky.

**3. Build in a human-only section.** Every task should have one part where AI is off-limits. Your own reflection. Your own example from your week. Your own opinion. This is where the real learning — and the real you — shows up.

## What this means for you

- **If you're a student or learner**: try the "thinking partner" approach. Use AI to brainstorm, write the draft yourself, then ask AI to poke holes in it. You'll learn faster, and the work will actually be yours.
- **If you're a manager or team leader**: stop writing policies that say "no AI." Instead, write ones that say "here's how we use AI together." Set clear rules — AI drafts, humans edit. AI summarises, humans decide. AI brainstorms, humans choose.
- **If you're just curious**: pick one task you do every week — a recurring report, a weekly email, a meal plan — and experiment with AI as a helper. Start small. See what works for you.

## Wrap-up

The smart move isn't to fight AI or hand everything over to it. It's to redesign the task so AI does what it's good at, and you do what only you can do. Pick one task today, try the "thinking partner" approach, and see how it feels. The work you produce will probably be better — and more yours — than either extreme would have given you.
